acceptanceCriteria.statement: The home screen presents the value proposition above the fold and keeps one primary call to action reachable without horizontal scrolling.
The pricing screen preserves tier hierarchy in a vertical mobile stack and keeps the comparison surface legible as the main decision area.
Navigation order and visible labeling remain consistent between home and pricing, with no hidden icon-only menu replacing the inspected structure.
Keyboard focus remains visible on navigation and primary action elements on both inspected routes.
The adapted surface does not reuse the source site’s proprietary wordmark, exact palette, or unique illustration treatments.

accessibilityAndRecovery: All interactive controls must preserve a visible keyboard focus state equivalent in clarity to the inspected pages.
Navigation labels should remain readable at the narrow sidebar width so first-time visitors can identify destinations without guessing.
If the viewport is too small for side-by-side pricing, tiers must stack in source order while keeping the first tier visually first.
If a user cannot immediately distinguish the primary action, the page must not introduce a second competing action; it should increase the contrast or prominence of the single primary action instead.
assumptions: The exact typography family and scale are not specified in the brief or evidence, so typography should be selected as an original system while preserving the observed hierarchy.
The precise content of the home hero and pricing tier labels is not provided, so copy should be rewritten generically rather than mirrored from the source snapshot.
The inspected snapshot does not disclose all navigation destinations, so only the retained ordering principle can be treated as fixed.

principles: Keep navigation destinations visible rather than hiding them behind a toggle, because the brief requires retention of the inspected navigation order and the evidence favors labeled sidebar navigation for first-visit clarity.
Use a single dominant call to action across home and pricing so the path to action is unambiguous and does not split attention across competing conversion buttons.
Preserve the hero’s first-screen hierarchy on home and the tier-comparison hierarchy on pricing, so the page still answers value-proposition and plan-comparison jobs in the expected order.
Use borders, rounded corners, and low elevation to separate panels and cards without borrowing branded illustration or palette choices from the source snapshot.
Let mobile behavior collapse into single-column stacks while keeping the same relative order of information, so the desktop structure remains recognizable on smaller screens.
globalDirection.summary: Retain the inspected site’s broad marketing structure: a fixed narrow navigation area with visible labels, a strong hero-first page hierarchy, and vertically stacked mobile flows. Rebuild the surface with an original visual language that uses borders and restrained fills to separate content, keeps one primary action across the experience, and preserves the pricing comparison as the main decision surface.

accessibility: Keep navigation labels visible so first-time visitors do not need to infer destinations from icons alone.
Maintain keyboard focus visibility on all interactive elements, including navigation links and the primary call to action.
Preserve a single, clearly distinguished primary action so assistive-technology users do not need to compare competing buttons.
failureAndRecovery: If the hero content overflows on small screens, stack the visual and copy blocks before the call to action rather than allowing horizontal scrolling.
If the primary action moves below the fold on mobile, pin the page flow so the action appears before any secondary content, not after it.
mobileRules: hero columns collapse to a single vertical stack at the mobile breakpoint
primary call to action remains reachable without horizontal scroll
screenBlueprints.summary: Home presents the value proposition above the fold with the navigation kept visible and the primary action reachable without lateral scrolling. The hero resolves into a single vertical stack on mobile while maintaining the same reading order.

accessibility: Make tier headers and price values visually distinct so the comparison can be scanned without relying on color alone.
Retain keyboard focus visibility across any price toggle, nav link, or CTA associated with pricing.
Keep structural boundaries on each tier so screen-reader and keyboard users can follow plan separation consistently.
failureAndRecovery: If comparison density becomes difficult on mobile, reduce parallelism by stacking tiers instead of compressing columns.
If a user opens pricing from home and needs to reverse course, keep navigation available without forcing page reloads or hidden menus.
mobileRules: pricing tiers stack vertically and preserve their tier hierarchy at the mobile breakpoint
screenBlueprints.summary: Pricing foregrounds a side-by-side comparison structure on larger screens and preserves tier hierarchy in a vertical stack on mobile. The page should keep the comparison surface dominant while the navigation remains visible for route changes back to home.

sourceDecisions.rationale: The inspected patterns consistently favor a fixed narrow sidebar with visible text labels, which preserves destination discoverability and route memory while keeping the main canvas available for marketing content.

The hero or top-of-page hierarchy should lead with the value proposition and keep a single primary action, because the brief requires home-page understanding above the fold and a single CTA from either inspected page.

Borders and rounded corners provide structure without making cards compete with the content they contain, which is appropriate for home sections and pricing panels in an original marketing adaptation.

The brief explicitly requires the home hero to collapse vertically on mobile and the pricing tiers to stack vertically while preserving hierarchy, so the adaptation should treat stacked flow as a core structural rule.

A single primary action should be carried across both inspected routes so the conversion path stays unambiguous; the source evidence supports single-CTA emphasis when a page must drive one dominant action.
The adaptation must avoid the source palette and proprietary branding, so the visual system should use original, generic color relationships rather than copying exact hues or branded accents.
Pricing is a comparison task, so the pricing page should prioritize the tier comparison surface and distinct header/body hierarchy rather than turning the cards into generic marketing blocks.
Icon-only navigation increases the learning burden for first-time visitors and conflicts with the brief’s requirement to retain clear navigation structure from the inspected pages.
Drop shadows and elevated cards would compete with the marketing content and pricing data, whereas the inspected evidence repeatedly favors boundaries that stay visually subordinate.
The case brief explicitly forbids inventing competing primary actions, and the evidence shows that a single CTA can reduce decision friction when the page must funnel toward one next step.
Pricing and marketing surfaces are not long-form data-entry flows, so heavy boxed form chrome would overstate interactivity and distract from route navigation and plan comparison.
